Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: always plan an escape route before entering a place
constantly scan environment for signs of threat
always sit with back against a wall to see the room

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.item: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, marked memory gaps alongside very easy verbal access to the trauma is a direct tension. Partial amnesia can coexist with being able to discuss some aspects, but as selected here the items imply opposing states of trauma recall and narrative access, making this node clinically incoherent.

'Incomprehensible chatter' is hard to reconcile with the listed military trauma context when the rest of the profile provides no corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content involving foreign-language confusion or crowd speech; it reads as a qualitatively different trauma cue from the other triggers.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'Triggered Without Warning' and 'Terror on Recall' at this severity level, because the memory profile otherwise suggests poorly integrated, highly affect-laden trauma recall rather than easy verbal access.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: Avoiding religious spaces is not well supported by the other selected triggers or memory items. There is no religious cue, appraisal, or memory content linking worship settings to the trauma, so this strategy appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: This item appears mis-specified for the node: it describes a trigger/context (being around authority figures or uniforms) rather than a maladaptive strategy/action the patient uses. Within the formulation, Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly linked, but the selected strategy items should still be coping behaviours. The other strategy items are behaviours (fawning, escape-route planning), whereas this item is a stimulus category, creating within-node incoherence and weakening alignment with the formulation.

For a military trauma profile centered on sensory-triggered re-experiencing, 'Alcohol smell' is not impossible, but it stands out as weakly anchored to the rest of the selected material. The other trigger and memory items suggest combat- or aircraft-related trauma cues and fragmented terror memory; alcohol odor implies a different trauma context unless there is additional explanation. This is not just unusual but clinically hard to integrate with the rest of the profile as presented.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened
issues.explanation: 'Fawn response' is the least coherent maladaptive strategy given the rest of the profile. The selected triggers and memory items point toward abrupt sensory flashbacks and hypervigilant danger-monitoring, which are well matched by checking surroundings and escape-route planning. Over-compliance as a threat response is more typically associated with interpersonal coercion dynamics and is not well linked to the chosen military/sensory trigger pattern or the active formulation, where Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly coupled in a vigilance/avoidance loop.

vignette: Amara was twenty-two when the armored vehicle hit a concealed charge on a desert highway. The concussive bang threw her forward, and through the swirling dust came the sharp, rising whine of helicopter rotors approaching. When she tried to push herself up, her palms caught on the coarse, sandpaper-like weave of a field casualty sling, the abrasive fibers biting into her skin as the heat washed over her. She could never quite string the event together for her family in Chicago or her medical instructors, drawing instead on the quiet endurance taught in her mother's kitchen and the disciplined training of the Army Reserve. The memory refused to take shape as a narrative; it existed only as a physical shock, a closed circuit that shorted whenever her body braced for impact again. She had come to believe that some things simply cannot be spoken, only carried. Over the following weeks and months, a quiet architecture of preparation accumulated. Before stepping through any doorway, her mind automatically traced the line of sight to the nearest exit, mapping two alternative paths in the time it took to inhale. She learned to scan every room the moment she crossed the threshold, her eyes moving in systematic arcs, cataloging furniture placement and light switches. She stopped meeting friends in round tables or open lounges; she always positioned herself with her spine flush against the wall, requiring a clear line of sight across the floor. The behaviors simply layered over her daily life. They were not decisions so much as reflexes that had taken up residence. At twenty-five, Amara works as a surgeon in a Chicago teaching hospital, a career that demands precision but inadvertently mirrors the conditions that triggered her nervous system. In the trauma bay, the coarse, stiff weave of the backup surgical drapes catches her fingertips and instantly floods her with the same terror she felt when the blast hit. She does not question the sensation; it simply arrives, heavy and inescapable, as if the floor is still giving way. When a nurse drops a steel instrument tray against the linoleum, the sharp crack triggers a full-body flinch before she can stop it, her breath catching in her throat as the room tilts. Outside the hospital's east wing, the low thrum of a news helicopter circling the skyline sounds like rotors, and Amara finds her shoulders hiking to her ears, her vision narrowing until she can focus only on the floor tiles. Her occupational environment now demands constant negotiation. Before entering the operating room, she walks the corridor twice, checking for service elevators and staff exits, her eyes tracking the movement of gurneys and crash carts. During preoperative briefings, she sits with her back pressed to the scrub sink wall, watching the surgical team enter from every angle. The accumulation of these habits has shaped her present. She goes home with her muscles tight, her mind still running the mental blueprints of the day, exhausted by the unbroken cycle of anticipation and alert. The weight of the load has grown heavier. Her presentation is marked by a steady, unyielding tension. The terror on recall does not fade with time; it remains vivid, arriving without warning whenever the world mimics that exact sequence of violence. The nonverbal memory persists as a physiological truth rather than a story. The triggers, safety behaviors, and intrusions coexist in her daily rhythm, each occupying its own space in her awareness. What finally brought her to seek clinical help was a Tuesday morning when she stood before a scrub sink, unable to recall which door led to the sterile storage wing, her hands trembling not from fatigue but from the sheer weight of constant vigilance. She realized she was operating one eye on the patient and the other on the perimeter. She came to the clinic hoping to quiet the static in her head, hoping to feel safe in a room where nothing is shooting or exploding, terrified that without the constant scanning and planned exits, she might be caught off guard again, and terrified that the memory she cannot speak will keep speaking through her nerves for the rest of her life.
